units.translation: of the gentle motion of wings. In some copies it has been changed to ψαύει [touches]. The later scholiast interprets both readings.
For the four-legged bird grazes the smooth path of the air with its wings.

Thus Blomfield for ψεκάς [drop]. The older form is ψακάς [drop] and ψακάζω [I drip], for which scribes often substituted ψεκάς [drop] and ψεκάζειν [to drip], as I have discussed in Thes. vol. 8 p. 1828. 1829.
He strikes me with a dark drop of bloody dew.

of the bonds to be placed on Prometheus, where the scholiast says: ψάλιά ἐστι κυρίως τὰ περιστόμια τῶν ἵππων [ψάλια are properly the muzzles of horses]. With this can be compared v. 562 τόνδε χαλινοῖς ἐν πετρίνοισιν χειμαζόμενον [this one storm-tossed in rocky bridles]. In the Guelferbytanus copy ψέλια [armlets], which I restored, since the following words show that it is said of armlets: βαλών νιν ἀμφὶ χερσὶν ἐγκρατεῖ σθένει ῥαιστῆρι θεῖνε, πασσάλευε πρὸς πέτραις [having cast them around his arms with mighty strength, strike with the hammer, nail him to the rocks].

This word is interpreted in various ways by the grammarians, on which see Thes. vol. 8 p. 1848. Hesychius explains it by ξηρόν [dry], αὐχμηρόν [parched], ἀσθενὲς [weak], ἐλαφρὸν [light], of which the last, ἐλαφρόν [light], is a fitting epithet for the ashes of a city devastated by fire
where the scholiast explained it by ἀσθενεῖ [weak], ἐλαφρᾷ [light].
